lesson.title: Keep connected things safe
lesson.subtitle: Default passwords, botnets, and how to lock a device down

video.title: Keep connected things safe
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talking to the student)

scenes.visual: Ms Salma at the school gate, arms folded, looking up at a new camera on a pole. A small sticker on the box reads admin.
scenes.animation: Push-in on the sticker; Ms Salma raises one eyebrow.
scenes.narration: Our new school gate camera came with the password “admin”. The installer shrugged: “They all do.” So anyone who knows that could look through it.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how attackers take over connected things, and how you keep yours safe.

scenes.visual: A row of identical cameras on a factory belt, each with the same tag: admin. A manual opens on a web page with the password in bold.
scenes.animation: Tags flip over one by one; the manual page scrolls to the password.
scenes.narration: Many devices leave the factory with the same password, like admin or one two three four. These defaults are in manuals anyone can find online. If nobody changes it, anyone can get in.

scenes.visual: A map of the world dotted with devices; a scanning beam sweeps across, and devices it touches flash briefly.
scenes.animation: The beam sweeps; a clock in the corner shows minutes ticking.
scenes.narration: Attackers don't try devices one by one. Programs scan the internet all day, knocking on millions of devices and trying factory passwords. A new camera can be found within minutes of going online.

scenes.visual: One camera gets a small red bot badge; then hundreds of cameras and routers light up with the same badge, linked by thin lines. In a house, a family watches TV, unaware.
scenes.animation: Badges spread like a wave; the family scene stays calm.
scenes.narration: A taken-over device can be controlled from far away. Join thousands of them, and you have a botnet: an army of hijacked devices. Their owners usually notice nothing.

scenes.visual: A short list of about 60 passwords on a card; a swarm of cameras and routers; well-known website tiles going grey with an offline sign.
scenes.animation: The list scrolls; the swarm grows; tiles grey out one by one.
scenes.narration: In twenty sixteen, the Mirai botnet did exactly this. With about sixty factory passwords, it took over hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers, then flooded big websites until they went offline.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph beside the swarm of hijacked devices. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! How did Mirai get into so many devices so easily?

scenes.visual: The factory password tags glow red; then a hand changes one tag, and that camera's bot badge falls away.
scenes.animation: Tags pulse; one tag flips to a long new password and the badge drops.
scenes.narration: Their owners kept the factory passwords. Mirai used no clever trick, just the defaults. That's good news: simple habits stop most attacks.

scenes.visual: A settings screen for a camera: the password field changes, an update toggle switches on, remote access switches off, and the camera moves to a separate guest network.
scenes.animation: Each setting changes as it is named, with a check mark.
scenes.narration: Here's how to lock a device down. Change the default password to a long new one. Turn on updates, which close the holes attackers use. Switch off what you don't use, like remote access. And put devices on their own network, like guest Wi-Fi.

scenes.visual: Left: short clever passwords crack in a flash. Right: a picture of a camel carrying a lantern by a river, with mint leaves, and the four words under it.
scenes.animation: The weak passwords shatter; the four words appear one by one.
scenes.narration: What makes a password strong? Length, not tricks. Programs try common words, and swaps like zero for O, almost at once. Four random words, like river camel lantern mint, are long and easy to remember.

scenes.visual: A camera with a microphone icon and a smart speaker with sound waves; a hand switches off the microphone, and the waves stop.
scenes.animation: The mic toggle flips off; a shield pops in.
scenes.narration: A device should also collect only what its job needs. A camera that records sound, or a speaker that's always listening, gathers far more. Switch off the rest: data that's never collected can never leak.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma at the gate again, pointing at the camera's small microphone. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Our gate camera can also record sound, but nobody needs it. What should the school do?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a key, an update arrow, a switch, a shield.
scenes.animation: Icons line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Switch the sound off: what's never recorded can never leak. Remember: change default passwords, update, switch off what you don't use, and collect only what's needed. Simple habits stop most attacks.

scenes.visual: A student and a parent at home looking at the router's settings page on a phone, ticking a short checklist.
scenes.animation: Three ticks appear on the checklist.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: a device check at home. With an adult, pick one device, like the Wi-Fi router. Check that its password was changed, updates are on, and nothing is on that nobody uses. Only check your own family's devices.

checkpoints.prompt: How did Mirai get into hundreds of thousands of devices so easily?

options.text: Their owners kept the factory passwords

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it simply typed in factory passwords that nobody had changed.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — Mirai cracked nothing clever. It tried about 60 factory passwords that owners had never changed.

checkpoints.prompt: The school's gate camera can also record sound, but nobody needs it. What should the school do?

options.text: Leave it on, just in case

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — sound that's never recorded can never leak, and a feature that's off can't be misused.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — “just in case” means collecting what the job doesn't need. Switch it off: what's never recorded can never leak.
